definition: Pliable means bending easily without breaking.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pliable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pliable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A good fly rod stays pliable at the tip, bowing deep with each strike instead of snapping.
Bendable says only that bending is possible — maybe with two hands and a knee; pliable means it gives easily, willingly, and takes no harm.
Limp overshoots pliable: the pliable reed bends and springs back to shape, while the limp one droops and offers nothing to push against.

Supple is softness with life in it — a dancer's back, worked leather, a willow wand — flexing smoothly and recovering on its own. It belongs to bodies and to living or leather-like things. Pliable is broader and plainer: anything that yields easily and without harm, from wire to a warmed hose.

Flexible is the broad, everyday word for whatever can adjust without breaking, and half its life is figurative — flexible schedules, flexible budgets, flexible thinking. Pliable stays closer to the physical act of yielding under pressure, and applied to a person it hints that they give in too readily.

Pliable means bending easily without breaking.
A garden hose forgotten on the January porch turns to a stubborn hoop, stiff as pipe — force a curve and it creases white, ready to split.
Carry it down to the warm cellar for an afternoon and it is pliable again, coiling smoothly around your arm and springing loose without a mark.
Pliable is the precise word because it prizes bending without damage: the hose curves, springs back, survives.
Its unit-mate malleable is about being reshaped for keeps — pressed into a new form that holds.
A pliable committee bends to the loudest voice this week and the next one next week; a malleable one is permanently remade by whoever pressed first.
Pliable is the word for easy, harmless bending — willow, a warmed hose, a rod tip — and, of people, for those who yield readily to pressure.
When the pressing is meant to leave a lasting new shape, its unit-mate malleable is more exact.
The two overlap on purpose; the spring-back belongs to pliable.

After a burn heals, the new skin wants to tighten.
Left alone, scar tissue draws in on itself like drying glue.
Therapists fight that tightening with massage, heat, and stretching, begun weeks before it might seem necessary.
The goal, therapists say, is to keep the healing tissue pliable — able to give under pressure and movement without tearing — so a wrist can still turn and a knuckle still fold.
Patients chart small victories: a jar opened, a shirt buttoned.
Each one means the tissue gave a little instead of resisting.
Skipped sessions show up fast.
Within weeks, tissue that once gave easily begins refusing, and motion shrinks with it.
